scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

However, keeping your son during her scheduled time isn’t achieving any of these goals in a healthy way. He could also develop resentment toward you or her, depending on how he perceives the situation. - **Relationship:** This could further damage your co-parenting relationship, making future agreements even harder to negotiate. --- ### **3. What Would Be a More Biblical and Wise Approach?** Here are some steps you could take, rooted in love, wisdom, and biblical principles: #### **A. Re-evaluate the Parenting Plan:** - **Advocate for a Fair Schedule:** If the current schedule isn’t working, consult with a family lawyer or mediator to request a modification. Explain that the current arrangement isn’t sustainable for you or your son. Set Boundaries with Your Ex:** - **Be Firm but Kind:** You don’t have to be a pushover, but you also don’t have to be confrontational. Can we reschedule for [specific time]?" - If she asks you to alter your time, say, "I can’t do that this time, but let’s discuss how we can make up for it later." - Avoid emotional reactions or ultimatums (e.g., "If you do this again, I’m keeping him"). - **Avoid Using Your Son as a Weapon:** Keeping your son to "punish" her is not loving or wise. It may feel satisfying in the moment, but it’s not a sustainable or healthy solution. #### **C. Protect Your Son’s Emotional Health:** - **Keep Him Out of the Conflict:** Avoid discussing your frustrations with him or making him feel like he’s "choosing" between you and his mother. This helps him feel secure. #### **D. Seek Wisdom and Support:** - **Talk to a Christian Counselor or Mentor:** A wise, godly person can help you navigate this situation with clarity and grace. They can also help you process your feelings of frustration and resentment in a healthy way. - **Pray for Guidance:** Ask God for wisdom (James 1:5) and for His peace (Philippians 4:6-7) as you navigate this. Pray for your ex as well—she’s also a parent, and she may be struggling in her own way. - **Consider Mediation:** If you’re stuck in a cycle of conflict, a neutral mediator (preferably one who understands Christian values) can help you and your ex find a compromise that works for your son. #### **E. Focus on Your Son’s Needs:** - **Prioritize His Joy and Security:** Your son is 8 years old—he likely doesn’t understand the complexities of your co-parenting dynamic. His primary need is to feel loved, secure, and connected to both of you. Even if the schedule isn’t perfect, try to make the time you have with him special and memorable. - **Avoid "Making Up" Time:** Trying to "make up" for lost time by keeping him during her scheduled time isn’t healthy. Instead, focus on making the time you *do* have with him count. For example: - Plan activities he enjoys. - Create traditions (e.g., a special dinner, a movie night). - Show up fully present when you’re with him. --- ### **4. Direct Answer to Your Question:** **Are you the "asshole" for keeping your son during her scheduled time?** In a practical and relational sense, **yes, this could be seen as the "asshole" move**—not because you’re wrong to want more time with your son, but because your method (withholding him to assert control) is not loving, wise, or sustainable. It risks: - Escalating conflict with your ex. - Harming your son’s emotional well-being. - Potentially violating court orders, which could have legal consequences. **A better approach** would be to: 1. **Advocate for a fairer parenting plan** through legal channels. 2. **Set firm but kind boundaries** with your ex about scheduling. 3. **Focus on making the time you have with your son meaningful** rather than trying to "win" time at her expense. 4. **Seek peace and reconciliation** (where possible) for your son’s sake. --- ### **5. Final Thoughts:** This situation is incredibly frustrating, and it’s easy to feel powerless or resentful. But as a Christian, your response should be rooted in love, patience, and a desire to honor God in how you treat others—even when they don’t treat you well. Your son is watching how you handle conflict, and he needs to see you modeling grace, self-control, and a commitment to his well-being above all else. If you’re feeling overwhelmed, I encourage you to: - Pray for guidance and strength. - Talk to a trusted Christian friend or mentor. - Consider professional help (e.g., counseling or mediation) to navigate this in a healthy way. You’re not alone in this, and God can give you the wisdom to handle this situation in a way that honors Him and protects your son.
